analysis.one_liner: Extends children's online privacy rules to teens and bans targeted ads aimed at kids.
analysis.headline: The Do Not Track Kids Act was introduced in May 2018, referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, and never received a hearing, vote, or floor action before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would update the children's online privacy law to cover teenagers ages 13 to 15, not just kids under 13. Websites and apps aimed at children or teens would need consent before collecting personal data, would be banned from using that data for targeted advertising to kids, and would have to give users tools to delete their content. Companies selling internet-connected toys and gadgets for kids would need to meet cybersecurity standards and disclose what data they collect.
analysis.who_benefits: Children and teenagers using websites, apps, games, and internet-connected toys — plus their parents, who would gain more control over what data is collected and the ability to get it deleted. Under the bill, teens themselves (not just parents) could control their own data.

how_it_helps.text: Extends online privacy protections from children under 13 to teenagers up to age 16, requiring notice and verifiable consent before collecting their personal information [S3].

Prohibits websites, apps, and connected devices aimed at kids or teens from using personal or geolocation information for targeted marketing — for children outright, and for teens without their consent [S3].
Requires operators to delete personal data on request and to offer users an 'eraser button' to remove posted content containing personal information [S3].

Bans the sale of internet-connected devices for children that fail FTC cybersecurity and data security standards, and requires a standardized 'privacy dashboard' on packaging showing what data the device collects [S3].
Lets state attorneys general sue to enforce the law and obtain damages or restitution for residents [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Internet companies, advertising networks, app developers, and makers of internet-connected toys and devices, which would face new limits on collecting and monetizing children's data and new security requirements.

drawbacks.text: The bill builds in self-regulation: companies could comply through industry-written 'safe harbor' guidelines approved by the FTC, with compliance deemed satisfied if they follow those guidelines [S3]. This softens the enforcement bite.

Coverage turns on whether a site or app is 'directed to' children or teens, with the FTC defining that term by regulation [S3]. Services not considered kid-directed could keep collecting teen data with only a knowledge-based trigger, limiting the practical reach.
Compliance costs for small app developers and device makers, and requirements like the eraser button are qualified 'to the extent technologically feasible' [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For families, the upside is straightforward: less tracking and advertising aimed at children, more parental and teen control over data, and baseline security for connected toys. The costs fall on companies that monetize children's attention and data. The bill's design has real soft spots — industry safe harbors and the 'directed to' trigger could narrow its effect — but its main provisions are clear and enforceable, and the benefits to children's privacy substantially outweigh the compliance burden.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee on the day it was introduced and sat there with no further action until Congress ended in January 2019 [S5].

narrative.text: Reps. Joe Barton (R-TX) and Bobby Rush (D-IL) introduced the bill on May 23, 2018 [S1].
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the same day [S5].
The 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019, with no further action taken on the bill [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies that profit from collecting children's and teens' data are better off because the bill never advanced — the current rules still cover only children under 13 and allow targeted advertising practices the bill would have restricted.

for.name: Rep. Joe Barton
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Do Not Track Kids Act of 2018 in the House [S1].

for.name: Rep. Bobby Rush
for.what_they_did: Joined as an original cosponsor at introduction, making the bill bipartisan from day one [S1].

sides.party_line_note: The bill was bipartisan from introduction (one Republican sponsor, one Democratic cosponsor), but it never reached a vote, so no one had to take a recorded position against it.

industries.note: The bill would bar them from collecting kids' and teens' personal data without consent and from using that data for targeted advertising, cutting into revenue built on tracking young users. It never advanced, so existing practices continued [S3].
Targeted marketing to children would have been prohibited outright, and to teens without their consent, restricting the audience data available to ad networks [S3].
Devices for children would have to meet FTC cybersecurity standards before sale and carry a privacy dashboard on the packaging; each noncompliant device could count as a separate violation [S3].
The bill would bring broadband and cable companies under FTC enforcement for children's privacy, closing an exemption that otherwise keeps them outside FTC privacy oversight [S3].
